subtopics.title: PN junction, depletion layer and barrier potential
subtopics.theory_md:
A **PN junction diode** is a p-type and an n-type semiconductor joined in one crystal: anode on the p side, cathode on the n side.

Holes diffuse from p to n and electrons from n to p, and recombine near the junction. This uncovers **fixed negative acceptor ions on the p side and fixed positive donor ions on the n side**. That region has no mobile carriers and is the **depletion layer**.

Its electric field opposes further diffusion. The potential across it is the **barrier potential**: about **0.7 V for Si and 0.3 V for Ge**.

Forward bias narrows the layer and current flows. Reverse bias widens it and only a tiny leakage flows, so the diode conducts in **one direction only**.
subtopics.basics_md: A semiconductor has two kinds of carriers: electrons (n-type) and holes (p-type). Put the two in contact and carriers near the boundary meet and cancel, like two crowds merging at a door. What is left behind is a thin strip of fixed charges, and that strip pushes back against more crowd crossing over.
key_points: PN diode = p-type joined to n-type; anode on p, cathode on n
Diffusion of majority carriers, recombination, fixed ions left behind: depletion layer
Field of the ions gives the barrier potential: Si 0.7 V, Ge 0.3 V
Forward bias narrows the layer, reverse bias widens it
Conducts in one direction only

questions.q: What is a PN junction diode? Explain how the depletion layer forms and what it does.
questions.model_answer_md:
**PN junction diode:** a p-type and an n-type semiconductor joined in one crystal, with anode on the p side and cathode on the n side.

**Formation of the depletion layer:**
1. Holes diffuse from p to n, electrons from n to p, and recombine near the junction.
2. This leaves fixed negative acceptor ions on the p side and fixed positive donor ions on the n side.
3. This charged region, free of mobile carriers, is the **depletion layer**.

**Effect:** its field opposes further diffusion and sets up the **barrier potential** (0.7 V Si, 0.3 V Ge). Forward bias narrows the layer and current flows; reverse bias widens it and the diode blocks, so it conducts one way only.
points: Definition: p-type and n-type joined, anode and cathode
Diffusion and recombination leave fixed ions
Depletion layer has no mobile carriers
Barrier potential 0.7 V Si, 0.3 V Ge

points: PN diode: p-type and n-type semiconductor joined in one crystal, anode and cathode

Forward bias: layer narrows, current flows once the barrier is overcome

Neat diagram of PN junction with depletion layer, fixed ions and barrier potential

Reverse bias: source adds to the barrier, layer widens, only the reverse saturation current (nA to $\mu$A)
Zener is always reverse biased because its useful action (constant voltage) occurs only in reverse breakdown
In forward bias a Zener acts as an ordinary diode with a drop of about 0.7 V, so it cannot regulate

subtopics.title: Forward and reverse V-I characteristics, breakdown
subtopics.theory_md:
**Forward bias** (anode to +): the source opposes the barrier and narrows the layer. Current is negligible until the **cut-in (knee) voltage** (Si 0.7 V, Ge 0.3 V), then rises steeply, limited only by the external resistance.

**Reverse bias:** the layer widens. A tiny **reverse saturation current** $I_0$ (nA for Si, $\mu$A for Ge) flows from **minority carriers**. It is nearly independent of voltage and doubles for every 10 °C.

At the **breakdown voltage** $V_{BR}$ the reverse current rises sharply (avalanche or Zener breakdown) and an ordinary diode is damaged unless the current is limited.

**Sketch:** forward quadrant in mA, reverse quadrant in $\mu$A, so the scales differ; mark $V_\gamma$, $I_0$ and $V_{BR}$. Equation: $I=I_0(e^{V/\eta V_T}-1)$.
subtopics.basics_md: Think of the junction as a one-way valve with a spring. In the forward direction you must push past the spring (the knee voltage) before water flows freely. In the reverse direction only a trickle leaks, until the pressure is so high that the valve bursts (breakdown).
key_points: Forward: negligible current below the knee voltage, then exponential rise
Reverse: small saturation current from minority carriers, nearly constant
Breakdown at $V_{BR}$: sharp rise in reverse current
Different scales for forward (mA) and reverse ($\mu$A) axes, labelled $V_\gamma$, $I_0$, $V_{BR}$
Circuit: diode, series resistor, variable supply, meters

questions.q: Why does the reverse current of a diode roughly double for every 10 °C rise, yet stay almost independent of the reverse voltage?
questions.model_answer_md:
**Cause of $I_0$:** minority carriers that are thermally generated near the junction and swept across by the barrier field.

**Temperature:** a higher temperature generates more electron-hole pairs, so $I_0$ increases; it roughly doubles for every 10 °C, $I_0(T_2)=I_0(T_1)\,2^{(T_2-T_1)/10}$.

**Voltage:** the number of minority carriers available is fixed by temperature, not by voltage. A small reverse voltage already sweeps all of them across, so a larger voltage adds nothing until breakdown.

Higher temperature generates more pairs, $I_0$ doubles per 10 °C

subtopics.title: Diode equation, resistance and temperature
subtopics.theory_md:
**Diode equation:** $I=I_0\left(e^{V/\eta V_T}-1\right)$ with $V_T=\dfrac{kT}{q}=\dfrac{T}{11600}\approx 26$ mV at 300 K. Rajput takes $\eta=1$ (Ge) and $2$ (Si); say which you assume. In forward bias $e^{V/\eta V_T}\gg1$, so $I\approx I_0e^{V/\eta V_T}$.

**Static resistance** $R=V/I$ at the operating point. **Dynamic resistance** $r_d=\dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta I}=\dfrac{\eta V_T}{I}$, which falls as the current rises.

**Temperature:** $I_0(T_2)=I_0(T_1)\,2^{(T_2-T_1)/10}$.

**Practical series circuit:** $I=\dfrac{V_s-V_\gamma}{R}$; reversed, the diode is open and drops all of $V_s$.
subtopics.basics_md: The diode equation just says current grows exponentially with voltage. Because the curve gets steeper as current rises, a small voltage change makes a big current change, so the diode's AC resistance gets smaller at higher current.
key_points: Static $R=V/I$; dynamic $r_d=\eta V_T/I$
$I_0$ doubles per 10 °C
Series circuit: subtract $V_\gamma$ before dividing by $R$

questions.q: Distinguish between static and dynamic resistance of a diode.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Static (DC) resistance:** $R_{DC}=V/I$ at the operating point, the slope of the line from the origin to that point.

**Dynamic (AC) resistance:** $r_d=\Delta V/\Delta I$, the reciprocal of the slope of the characteristic at the point, and $r_d=\eta V_T/I$. It is small in forward bias and decreases as current rises; it applies to small AC signals.

subtopics.title: Zener diode, Zener and avalanche breakdown
subtopics.theory_md:
A **Zener diode** is a heavily doped silicon diode made to work in reverse **breakdown**. There its voltage stays nearly constant at $V_Z$ over a wide current range, so it is a voltage reference. It is always reverse biased (cathode to +); forward, it is an ordinary diode with a 0.7 V drop.

**Zener breakdown:** heavy doping, thin depletion layer, intense field pulls electrons out of bonds (field emission), $V_Z$ below about 5 V, **negative** temperature coefficient.

**Avalanche breakdown:** light doping, wide layer, minority carriers gain energy and knock out more carriers (impact ionisation), $V_Z$ above about 6 V, **positive** temperature coefficient.

Characteristic: sharp knee at $V_Z$, between $I_{Z,min}$ and $I_{Z,max}$.
subtopics.basics_md: Every diode eventually breaks down if the reverse voltage is high enough. A Zener is built so that this happens at a chosen, repeatable voltage and does no damage as long as a resistor limits the current. Above the breakdown point the voltage barely moves while the current changes a lot, which is what makes it a voltage reference.
key_points: Zener: heavily doped diode used in reverse breakdown, current limited by a resistor
Zener breakdown: heavy doping, thin layer, field emission, low $V_Z$, negative temperature coefficient
Avalanche breakdown: light doping, wide layer, impact ionisation, higher $V_Z$, positive temperature coefficient
Characteristic: constant $V_Z$ between $I_{Z,min}$ and $I_{Z,max}$

questions.why: Only in breakdown is the voltage nearly constant over a wide current range.

questions.why: Wide layer and light doping give impact ionisation, which is avalanche.

questions.q: Distinguish between Zener breakdown and avalanche breakdown.
questions.model_answer_md:
| Zener breakdown | Avalanche breakdown |
|---|---|
| Heavily doped junction | Lightly doped junction |
| Thin depletion layer | Wide depletion layer |
| Strong field breaks covalent bonds directly (field emission) | Accelerated carriers knock out electrons by collision (impact ionisation) |
| $V_Z$ below about 5 V | $V_Z$ above about 6 V |
| Negative temperature coefficient | Positive temperature coefficient |
points: Mechanism: field emission vs impact ionisation

questions.why: Below about 5 V the Zener mechanism dominates, which has a negative coefficient.

questions.q: Draw and explain the V-I characteristic of a Zener diode. Why is it always used in reverse bias?
questions.model_answer_md:
**Characteristic:** in forward bias it is an ordinary diode (knee about 0.7 V). In reverse bias a small leakage current flows until $V_Z$; there the current rises almost vertically, so the voltage stays near $V_Z$ for any current from $I_{Z,min}$ (knee) to $I_{Z,max}$ (power limit, $P_Z=V_ZI_Z$).

**Why reverse biased:** its useful action, constant voltage at changing current, exists only in breakdown. In forward bias it just drops 0.7 V and cannot regulate. A series resistor is needed to limit the current in breakdown.
points: Sketch: forward knee 0.7 V, reverse breakdown at $V_Z$ nearly vertical
Constant voltage action only in reverse breakdown

subtopics.title: Zener shunt voltage regulator
subtopics.theory_md:
**Circuit:** unregulated $V_{in}$ feeds a series resistor $R_S$; the Zener (reverse biased) and the load $R_L$ are in parallel across the output, so $V_o=V_Z$.

$$I_S=\frac{V_{in}-V_Z}{R_S},\quad I_L=\frac{V_Z}{R_L},\quad I_Z=I_S-I_L,\quad P_Z=V_ZI_Z$$

**Line regulation:** $V_{in}$ rises, $I_S$ rises, the extra current goes through the Zener and the extra drop is across $R_S$; $V_o$ stays $V_Z$.

**Load regulation:** $R_L$ falls, $I_L$ rises and $I_Z$ falls by the same amount; $I_S$ is unchanged.

**Limits:** $I_Z\ge I_{Z,min}$, so $R_{L,min}=\dfrac{V_Z}{I_S-I_{Z,min}}$; and $P_Z\le P_{Z,max}$ at maximum $V_{in}$ and minimum load.
subtopics.basics_md: The Zener holds the output at a fixed voltage by acting as a current sponge. The resistor in series takes whatever voltage is left over, and the Zener soaks up whatever current the load does not use.
key_points: Zener in parallel with the load, reverse biased, with a series resistor $R_S$
$I_S=(V_{in}-V_Z)/R_S$, $I_L=V_Z/R_L$, $I_Z=I_S-I_L$
Line and load regulation by the change in $I_Z$
Regulation lost if $I_Z$ falls to zero: $R_{L,min}$
$P_Z=V_ZI_Z$ must stay below the rating

questions.q: Explain with a circuit how a Zener diode regulates the output voltage against changes in input voltage and load.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Circuit:** $V_{in}$, series resistor $R_S$, then the Zener (cathode to the positive side) in parallel with $R_L$; $V_o=V_Z$.

**Input change:** if $V_{in}$ rises, $I_S$ rises; $I_L=V_Z/R_L$ is fixed, so the extra current flows through the Zener and the extra voltage drops across $R_S$. $V_o$ stays $V_Z$.

**Load change:** if $R_L$ falls, $I_L$ rises and $I_Z$ falls by the same amount; $I_S$ and the drop across $R_S$ are unchanged, so $V_o$ is constant.

**Limit:** $I_Z$ must remain above $I_{Z,min}$.
points: Circuit: $R_S$ in series, Zener reverse biased in parallel with load
Input rise: extra current through Zener, extra drop across $R_S$

questions.q: For the regulator of $V_{in}=18$ V, $R_S=300\ \Omega$, $V_Z=12$ V, find the smallest load resistance that keeps regulation if $I_{Z,min}=2$ mA.
questions.model_answer_md:
$I_S=20$ mA is fixed.

Maximum load current: $I_{L,max}=I_S-I_{Z,min}=20-2=18$ mA

$R_{L,min}=\dfrac{V_Z}{I_{L,max}}=\dfrac{12}{0.018}=667\ \Omega$

topics.topic: Half wave and full wave rectifiers

subtopics.title: Half-wave rectifier
subtopics.theory_md:
One diode in series with the load. It conducts in the positive half cycle only, so the output is one hump per cycle and $f_{out}=f$.

With $v=V_m\sin\omega t$ and $I_m=\dfrac{V_m}{r_f+R_L}$:

$$I_{dc}=\frac{I_m}{\pi},\quad I_{rms}=\frac{I_m}{2},\quad V_{dc}=I_{dc}R_L$$

For an ideal diode $V_{dc}=V_m/\pi$ and $V_{rms}=V_m/2$. **PIV $=V_m$**. Ripple factor 1.21 and maximum efficiency 40.6%; transformer utilisation factor 0.287. Disadvantages: high ripple, DC in the transformer secondary can saturate the core, poor utilisation.

Convert first: $V_m=\sqrt2\,V_{rms}$.
subtopics.basics_md: The diode lets current through only one way, so during the negative half of the AC wave nothing reaches the load. Averaging one hump over a whole cycle (hump plus a flat gap) gives $V_m/\pi$.
key_points: One diode, conducts in the positive half cycle only
$I_{dc}=I_m/\pi$, $I_{rms}=I_m/2$, $V_{dc}=V_m/\pi$ (ideal)
PIV $=V_m$, ripple frequency $f$
$V_m=\sqrt2\,V_{rms}$ before using any formula

subtopics.title: Full-wave centre-tap rectifier
subtopics.theory_md:
**Circuit:** transformer with a centre-tapped secondary; D1 at one end, D2 at the other, cathodes joined to $R_L$, whose other end goes to the centre tap. Each half supplies $V_m\sin\omega t$.

**Working:** positive half cycle, D1 conducts and D2 is off; negative half cycle, D2 conducts and D1 is off. The load current has the **same direction** in both, so $f_{out}=2f$. The off diode sees the whole secondary: **PIV $=2V_m$**.

With $i=I_m|\sin\theta|$ (period $\pi$), $I_m=\dfrac{V_m}{r_f+R_L}$:

$I_{dc}=\dfrac{2I_m}{\pi}$, $I_{rms}=\dfrac{I_m}{\sqrt2}$, $\eta=\dfrac{0.812}{1+r_f/R_L}$, $\gamma=0.482$.

Waveforms: input, $i_{D1}$, $i_{D2}$ and load, aligned in time.
subtopics.basics_md: A centre-tap transformer gives two equal AC voltages that are always opposite in sign. One diode catches the positive swing of the top half; the other catches the positive swing of the bottom half, so the load gets a hump every half cycle instead of every cycle.
key_points: Two diodes, centre-tapped secondary, each half gives $V_m$
D1 conducts in the positive half cycle, D2 in the negative; load current same direction
$I_{dc}=2I_m/\pi$, $I_{rms}=I_m/\sqrt2$, $V_{dc}=2V_m/\pi$
PIV $=2V_m$, $f_{out}=2f$
Efficiency $0.812/(1+r_f/R_L)$, ripple factor 0.482

questions.q: A centre-tap full-wave rectifier has a 12-0-12 V rms secondary (12 V rms on each half), ideal diodes and $R_L=100\ \Omega$. Find $V_{dc}$, $I_{dc}$ and the PIV.

**Given:** each half is 12 V rms, so $V_m=\sqrt2\times12=16.97$ V per half.

$V_{dc}=\dfrac{2V_m}{\pi}=\dfrac{2\times16.97}{\pi}=10.80\ \text{V}$

$I_{dc}=\dfrac{V_{dc}}{R_L}=\dfrac{10.80}{100}=108\ \text{mA}$

$\text{PIV}=2V_m=2\times16.97=33.9\ \text{V}$

questions.q: Sketch and describe the waveforms of the input, the diode currents $i_{D1}$, $i_{D2}$ and the load current in a centre-tap full-wave rectifier.

1. **Input:** sine wave $V_m\sin\omega t$.
2. **$i_{D1}$:** half-sine humps only for $0$ to $T/2$.
3. **$i_{D2}$:** half-sine humps only for $T/2$ to $T$.
4. **Load current:** a hump in every half cycle (sum of the two), all in the same direction, frequency $2f$.

Load current is a hump every half cycle, same direction
Neat circuit: centre-tapped transformer, D1, D2, $R_L$ to the centre tap

subtopics.title: Bridge rectifier and why it is preferred
subtopics.theory_md:
**Circuit:** four diodes D1 to D4. The AC secondary is across one diagonal and $R_L$ across the other; no centre tap.

**Positive half cycle:** D1 and D3 conduct, D2 and D4 are off. **Negative half cycle:** D2 and D4 conduct. Current through $R_L$ is in the same direction both times, $f_{out}=2f$.

$V_{dc}=\dfrac{2V_m}{\pi}$, $I_{rms}=\dfrac{I_m}{\sqrt2}$, **PIV $=V_m$**, TUF 0.812.

With practical diodes **two** conduct in series: $V_m'=V_m-2V_\gamma$ and the diode resistance is $2r_f$.

**Why preferred over centre-tap:** no centre-tapped transformer, PIV $V_m$ instead of $2V_m$, whole secondary used (twice the $V_{dc}$ for the same secondary voltage), better TUF. Cost: four diodes and two drops.
subtopics.basics_md: In a bridge, the four diodes steer current like a road junction with one-way streets: whichever way the AC pushes, the current is routed through the load in the same direction. This lets the whole secondary winding work on both half cycles, with no centre tap.
key_points: Four diodes; D1, D3 conduct in the positive half cycle, D2, D4 in the negative
Load current same direction both times; $f_{out}=2f$
$V_{dc}=2V_m/\pi$, PIV $=V_m$
Practical: two drops $2V_\gamma$ and $2r_f$
Preferred: no centre tap, lower PIV, higher TUF (0.812)

subtopics.title: Ripple factor
subtopics.theory_md:
**Ripple factor** is the ratio of the rms value of the AC component of the output to its DC value:

$$\gamma=\frac{I_{ac}}{I_{dc}}=\sqrt{\left(\frac{I_{rms}}{I_{dc}}\right)^2-1}=\sqrt{k_f^2-1}$$

since $I_{rms}^2=I_{dc}^2+I_{ac}^2$ and $k_f=I_{rms}/I_{dc}$ is the form factor. Smaller is better.

- **Half wave:** $I_{dc}=I_m/\pi$, $I_{rms}=I_m/2$, $k_f=1.57$, $\gamma=1.21$.
- **Full wave:** $I_{dc}=2I_m/\pi$, $I_{rms}=I_m/\sqrt2$, $k_f=1.11$, $\gamma=0.482$.

Ripple voltage $V_{r,rms}=\gamma V_{dc}$. Capacitor filter, full wave: $\gamma\approx\dfrac{1}{4\sqrt3\,fCR_L}$ (half wave: $\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt3\,fCR_L}$).
subtopics.basics_md: The output of a rectifier is a steady part (DC) plus a wobble (AC). The ripple factor says how big the wobble is compared with the steady part. A perfect battery has zero ripple.
key_points: Definition: rms of AC component divided by DC value
$\gamma=\sqrt{(I_{rms}/I_{dc})^2-1}$
Half wave 1.21, full wave 0.482
$V_{r,rms}=\gamma V_{dc}$
Ripple depends only on the waveform, not on $R_L$ or $r_f$

Show that the ripple factor is $\gamma=\sqrt{(I_{rms}/I_{dc})^2-1}$ and evaluate it for a full-wave rectifier.
questions.model_answer_md:
The output has a DC part and an AC part, so $I_{rms}^2=I_{dc}^2+I_{ac}^2$.

$\gamma=\dfrac{I_{ac}}{I_{dc}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{I_{rms}^2-I_{dc}^2}}{I_{dc}}=\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{I_{rms}}{I_{dc}}\right)^2-1}$

Full wave: $I_{rms}/I_{dc}=\dfrac{I_m/\sqrt2}{2I_m/\pi}=\dfrac{\pi}{2\sqrt2}=1.11$, so $\gamma=\sqrt{1.11^2-1}=0.482$.

questions.q: The DC output of an unfiltered full-wave rectifier is 20 V. Find the rms ripple voltage. What would it be for a half-wave rectifier with the same DC output?
questions.model_answer_md:
$V_{r,rms}=\gamma V_{dc}$

Full wave: $0.482\times20=9.6$ V (rms), at 100 Hz for a 50 Hz supply.

Half wave: $1.21\times20=24.2$ V (rms), at 50 Hz.

questions.q: A full-wave rectifier with a capacitor filter of 1000 $\mu$F feeds $R_L=500\ \Omega$ from 50 Hz mains. Find the ripple factor.

$\gamma=\dfrac{1}{4\sqrt3\,fCR_L}=\dfrac{1}{4\sqrt3\times50\times1000\times10^{-6}\times500}$

$fCR_L=50\times10^{-3}\times500=25$, so $\gamma=\dfrac{1}{6.928\times25}=0.00577\approx0.58\%$

subtopics.title: Rectification efficiency and derivations
subtopics.theory_md:
**Efficiency** $\eta=\dfrac{P_{dc}}{P_{ac}}$ with $P_{dc}=I_{dc}^2R_L$ and $P_{ac}=I_{rms}^2(r_f+R_L)$.

**Script for any derivation:** write $i=I_m\sin\theta$ over the conduction interval, integrate for $I_{dc}$ and $I_{rms}$, substitute.

- **Half wave:** $\eta=\dfrac{(I_m/\pi)^2R_L}{(I_m/2)^2(r_f+R_L)}=\dfrac{4}{\pi^2}\dfrac{1}{1+r_f/R_L}=\dfrac{0.406}{1+r_f/R_L}$, maximum **40.6%**.
- **Full wave (CT or bridge):** $\eta=\dfrac{(2I_m/\pi)^2R_L}{(I_m/\sqrt2)^2(r_f+R_L)}=\dfrac{8}{\pi^2}\dfrac{1}{1+r_f/R_L}=\dfrac{0.812}{1+r_f/R_L}$, maximum **81.2%** (when $r_f\ll R_L$).
- **Bridge:** two diodes conduct, so replace $r_f$ by $2r_f$.
subtopics.basics_md: Efficiency is simply the DC power delivered to the load divided by the AC power drawn in. Some AC power is wasted in the diode resistance, and part of the output is AC wobble that does no DC work, so even an ideal rectifier is not 100% efficient.
key_points: $\eta=P_{dc}/P_{ac}=I_{dc}^2R_L/[I_{rms}^2(r_f+R_L)]$
Bridge uses $2r_f$ (two diodes in series)
Derivation: integrate $I_{dc}$ and $I_{rms}$, then substitute

questions.q: A half-wave rectifier has $r_f=50\ \Omega$ and $R_L=450\ \Omega$. Its efficiency is about
Derive the expression for the rectification efficiency of a half-wave rectifier and state its maximum value.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Setup:** $v=V_m\sin\theta$, diode resistance $r_f$, load $R_L$. The current is $i=I_m\sin\theta$ for $0\le\theta\le\pi$ and zero for $\pi\le\theta\le2\pi$, with $I_m=V_m/(r_f+R_L)$.

**DC current:** $I_{dc}=\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^\pi I_m\sin\theta\,d\theta=\dfrac{I_m}{\pi}$

**RMS current:** $I_{rms}^2=\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^\pi I_m^2\sin^2\theta\,d\theta=\dfrac{I_m^2}{4}$, so $I_{rms}=\dfrac{I_m}{2}$

**Powers:** $P_{dc}=I_{dc}^2R_L=\dfrac{I_m^2R_L}{\pi^2}$, $P_{ac}=I_{rms}^2(r_f+R_L)=\dfrac{I_m^2}{4}(r_f+R_L)$

**Efficiency:** $\eta=\dfrac{P_{dc}}{P_{ac}}=\dfrac{4}{\pi^2}\cdot\dfrac{R_L}{r_f+R_L}=\dfrac{0.406}{1+r_f/R_L}$

**Maximum** ($r_f\ll R_L$): **40.6%**.

questions.q: A full-wave bridge rectifier has a peak secondary voltage of 30 V, diode resistance 10 $\Omega$ each and $R_L=190\ \Omega$ (ideal otherwise). Find $I_{dc}$, $V_{dc}$ and the efficiency.
questions.model_answer_md:
Two diodes conduct in series, so the resistance in the path is $2r_f+R_L=20+190=210\ \Omega$.

$I_m=\dfrac{30}{210}=142.9\ \text{mA}$

$I_{dc}=\dfrac{2I_m}{\pi}=90.9\ \text{mA}$, $V_{dc}=I_{dc}R_L=17.3\ \text{V}$

$\eta=\dfrac{0.8106}{1+2r_f/R_L}=\dfrac{0.8106}{1+20/190}=73.3\%$

points: Bridge: two diodes conduct, so total resistance $2r_f+R_L$

subtopics.title: Numericals with winding resistance, diode resistance and cut-in voltage
subtopics.theory_md:
**Method** for the usual 5-mark numerical, with $n=1$ for half wave and centre-tap, $n=2$ for a bridge:

1. $V_m=\sqrt2\,V_{rms}$ (for a centre-tap, per half of the secondary).
2. $I_m=\dfrac{V_m-nV_\gamma}{R_s+n\,r_f+R_L}$ ($V_\gamma=0$ if not given).
3. $I_{dc}=\dfrac{I_m}{\pi}$ (HW) or $\dfrac{2I_m}{\pi}$ (FW); $V_{dc}=I_{dc}R_L$.
4. $P_{dc}=I_{dc}^2R_L$; $P_{ac}=I_{rms}^2(R_s+nr_f+R_L)+nV_\gamma I_{dc}$; $\eta=P_{dc}/P_{ac}$.
5. $\gamma=1.21$ (HW) or $0.482$ (FW): waveform only.
6. Regulation: $\%\text{Reg}=\dfrac{V_{NL}-V_{FL}}{V_{FL}}\times100=\dfrac{R_s+nr_f}{R_L}\times100$.
subtopics.basics_md: Treat every resistance in the conducting path as one total series resistance, and every cut-in voltage as a battery that eats into the peak voltage. Then the current is just Ohm's law at the peak, and the averaging factors ($1/\pi$ or $2/\pi$) turn peak into DC.

Define voltage regulation of a rectifier. How does it come out as $(R_s+r_f)/R_L$?
questions.model_answer_md:
**Voltage regulation** is the fall in DC output voltage from no load to full load, as a percentage of the full-load value:

$\%\text{Reg}=\dfrac{V_{NL}-V_{FL}}{V_{FL}}\times100$

Ignoring $V_\gamma$: at no load there is no drop, so $V_{NL}=V_m/\pi$ (half wave). On load the DC current flows through $R_s$ and $r_f$, so $V_{FL}=V_{NL}\dfrac{R_L}{R_s+r_f+R_L}$. Then $\dfrac{V_{NL}-V_{FL}}{V_{FL}}=\dfrac{R_s+r_f}{R_L}$. A smaller value is better.
points: Definition: (no-load minus full-load voltage) over full-load voltage, times 100

Bridge: $V_m=\sqrt2\times14.14=20$ V; two diodes in series so $2r_f=30\ \Omega$
